newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Drop in Dutch call money rates has market gasping.
newsitem.headline: Drop in Dutch call money rates has market gasping.

text.p: Dutch call money rates nosedived on Tuesday morning and started bottoming out in early afternoon, leaving the market gasping after the unexpected drop.

One dealer said the sharp fall in call money rates looked to have prompted a slight panic in the market, but added that volumes were light and overnight money should rise to its usual level of around 3.00 percent bid on Thursday.
The Dutch markets are closed on Wednesday, Queen's Day.
Call money was bid at 1.75 percent in late morning trade, but edged up a little to 2.00 percent in early afternoon.
One dealer said there was a big bank shedding liquidity as it had been saving too much under the current credit quota.
Banks can build up savings under the quota as the central bank sets a daily average for commercial banks' borrowing at the secured loans rate, currently 2.50 percent.
"It is very unusual," another dealer said, arguing the secured loans rate was higher than the price for overnight money so that the bank concerned would lose on the deal.
Call money was quoted at 1.75/2.25 percent bid/offer in late morning trade versus 3.06/18 on Monday.
Dealers said that this morning's allocation of 2.33 billion guilders under the new advances pact had not been excessive.
"The drop in call money rates is not a result of this morning's allocation, as that could better be described as tight than ample, particularly because markets are closed on Wednesday," one said.
Another dealer said the month-end effect was pushing call money rates lower.
"There must be a big player in the market who has too much liquidity," he said. He said call money rates were expected to return to normal on Thursday at the start of the new month.
Other rates were virtually unchanged. Three-month deposits were bid at a stable 3.12 percent bid.
One-year paper rose two basis points to 3.34 percent bid.
The guilder was somewhat stronger against the German mark, quoting at 112.485 per 100 marks versus 112.50 on Monday.
